Abstract
Background  Acute pancreatitis (AP) is a common gastrointestinal disease prone to severe systemic complications, 
presenting with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis depends on serum markers and imaging. 
Categorized by the Atlanta classification, about 20% of cases progress to more severe forms. Due to its rapid 
progression and high misdiagnosis rate, early and accurate assessment is crucial. In this study, we aim to construct a 
deep neural network to provide a scientific basis for the clinical management of AP.
Methods  A total of 1,884 patients diagnosed with AP from four hospitals, namely the Fourth Affiliated Hospital 
of Zhejiang University School of Medicine(ZJU-H4), the First Affiliated Hospital of Ningbo University(NBU-H1), the 
Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University(ZCMU-H2), and Lishui People’s Hospital(LISHUI-H), 
were retrospectively included from 2012 to 2024. The examination indicators of the patients within 48 h and 72 h 
after admission were collected. Clinical models were developed using Arya, a novel privacy computing platform by 
Healink to predict the severity of AP in patients. Two learning methods—logistic regression (LR) and deep neural 
networks (DNN)—were applied within the federated learning framework. Moreover, to address the challenge of 
fair contribution evaluation in federated learning, a novel assessment method integrating data quality and model 
performance impact was proposed.
Results  In the 48-hour scenario, the DNN model showed higher prediction performance than the logistic regression 
model in terms of sensitivity (78.20% vs. 78.70%), specificity (78.40% vs. 72.90%) and accuracy (78.30% vs. 75.90%); the 
same trend was observed in the 72-hour scenario: sensitivity (78.10% vs. 83.30%), specificity (80.90% vs. 70.60%) and 
accuracy (79.40% vs. 77.10%). Moreover, the model based on data within 72 h was more accurate than that within

Key findings
• We constructed deep neural network models using data from 1884 AP 
patients from four hospitals. In both 48 - hour and 72 - hour scenarios, 
DNN outperformed logistic regression in predicting AP severity. The 
DNN - based model using 72 - hour - after - admission indicators was 
the most accurate.
What is known and what is new?
• Known: Some serological indicators help evaluate AP severity but 
have limitations. Existing scoring systems have many items and poor 
operability.
• New: We integrated data from multiple institutions via federated 
learning on a privacy - computing platform. We also proposed a new 
contribution evaluation method for fairer federated learning.
What is the implication, and what should change now?
• Implications: Our study enables more accurate early prediction of 
AP severity, ensuring patient privacy. The new evaluation method 
promotes fairer multi - center collaboration.
• Actions needed: Clinicians can use our model for better AP manage­
ment. More institutions could adopt federated learning with our evalu­
ation method for future research.
Introduction
Acute pancreatitis [1] (AP) is a common gastrointestinal 
disease that can easily lead to severe systemic complica­
tions. Its clinical manifestations mainly include abdomi­
nal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Clinical diagnosis relies 
on serum amylase, lipase, and abdominal CT. As of 2019, 
the global incidence rate [2] of AP was 3.48 per 10,000. 
According to the Atlanta classification [3], AP can be 
divided into mild acute pancreatitis (MAP), moderately 
severe acute pancreatitis (MSAP), and severe acute pan­
creatitis (SAP). This classification depends on the extent 
of local damage within and around the pancreas and sys­
temic damage to distant organs. MAP is characterized 
by pancreatic hyperemia and edema at the tissue level. 
The course of the disease is often self - limiting, and it 
accounts for the majority of AP patients, generally with 
a good prognosis. Approximately 20% of patients will 
develop into moderately severe or severe cases, with a 
significantly higher incidence of local and systemic com­
plications and mortality rates [4]. At the same time, the 
condition of patients with AP often progresses rapidly, 
making early misdiagnosis common. Therefore, early, 
accurate, and timely assessment is crucial for AP patients, 
which is the key to reducing mortality.
Previous studies have confirmed that certain serologi­
cal indicators are of significance in evaluating the severity 
of AP, but there are still some limitations. For example, 
although there is a correlation between hematocrit 
(HCT), blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and the severity of 
AP, their accuracy in independently diagnosing SAP is 
poor [5]. C - reactive protein (CRP) is an acute - phase 
reaction indicator under the condition of inflammation 
and/or infection in the body, which is simple and easy to 
measure [6]. However, a continuous increase or a value 
greater than 150 mg/L after 72 h of onset is required to 
achieve high accuracy in diagnosing pancreatic necro­
sis [7] Currently, the commonly used scoring systems in 
clinical practice include Ranson score, CT severity index 
(CTSI) score, bedside index for severity in acute pancre­
atitis (BISAP) score, and acute physiology and chronic 
health evaluation (APACHE II) score. One or more of 
these prediction methods can be combined to plan the 
initial care and intervention levels required for patient 
management during the disease process. However, the 
limitation lies in the large number of involved items, 
resulting in poor clinical operability [1]Therefore, we 
hope to construct a simpler, more accurate, specific, and 
efficient model to predict the severity of AP at an early 
stage, providing a basis for formulating reasonable clini­
cal plans.
In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) technology 
has been widely applied in the medical field. With the 
advent of the big - data era and the rapid development of 
informatization, a large amount of complex medical data 
has been generated for clinical work. The latest research 
focuses on tracking and processing patients’ electronic 
health records, and using machine - learning and data 
- mining techniques to develop highly accurate risk - 
assessment models [8].Machine learning is an interdisci­
plinary field. By simulating the human way of thinking, 
it relies on a large amount of training data to learn and 
improve itself, gradually enhances its performance, and 
makes complex decisions based on the learning behavior 
[9].
Although predictive models based on machine learn­
ing have good application prospects in assisting medical 
diagnosis, they require a large amount of relevant data for 
training to achieve good diagnostic results. Moreover, such 
predictive models may rely on confounding factors related 
48 h. The optimal model among the four scenarios was the DNN - based model using indicators within 72 h after 
admission.
Conclusion  This study successfully integrated collective knowledge and data resources from various medical 
institutions while ensuring patient privacy and data security through the adoption of federated learning. It 
demonstrated a significant leap in the prediction of AP severity using machine learning. Furthermore, by introducing 
a novel contribution evaluation mechanism, it addressed the limitations of traditional data-sharing methods, 
enhancing fairness and incentivizing multi-center participation.

to institutional bias rather than making predictions based 
on pathology. When tested with data from the same hos­
pital, the model may show high accuracy, but it cannot 
be well generalized to external hospitals or even different 
departments within the same hospital [10]. The solution to 
the problem of data scale and diversity is distributed col­
laborative learning, that is, using data from multiple institu­
tions to train the same model. However, since patient data 
is private and cannot be shared across institutions or even 
departments, there is a problem of patient data silos [11], 
which hinders the smooth progress of distributed training.
Federated learning [12] is a collaborative learning 
method that respects data privacy. It aims to address the 
issues of data security and privacy protection through 
collaborative training without the need to exchange the 
underlying datasets. This means that federated learning 
enables cross - institutional collaborative training with­
out sharing patient data. Recent research has shown [13] 
hat this approach can achieve performance comparable 
to that of training with a centralized database and out­
performs models based on data from any single medical 
institution. However, in federated learning-based multi-
center collaboration, fair evaluation of each center’s con­
tribution remains a challenge, as existing methods often 
rely solely on data volume and overlook the impact of 
data quality and actual model performance. To address 
this, our study proposes a novel contribution evaluation 
method that innovatively integrates data quality (encom­
passing timeliness, completeness, and scarcity) and 
model performance impact (quantified through marginal 
loss changes across iterations). This dual-dimensional 
framework enables a more comprehensive and objective 
assessment of each center’s contribution, which is a key 
novelty compared to traditional single-factor evaluation 
approaches.
The aim of this study is to predict the severity of 
patients with acute pancreatitis using a multi - center 
joint modeling approach based on real - world clinical 
scenarios. Additionally, we will evaluate the prediction 
effects of different prediction methods under different 
time windows, so as to provide a scientific basis for the 
clinical management of acute pancreatitis.
Materials and methods
Participants and inclusion criteria
A total of 2,012 patients with first - onset AP who were 
hospitalized from January 1, 2012, to December 31, 2024, 
in the Fourth Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University 
School of Medicine(ZJU-H4), the First Affiliated Hospi­
tal of Ningbo University(NBU-H1), the Second Affiliated 
Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University(ZCMU-
H2), and Lishui People’s Hospital(LISHUI-H) were 
retrospectively selected as the study subjects. All four 
hospitals are Class - III Grade - A hospitals, equipped 
with a comprehensive diagnosis and treatment system for 
acute pancreatitis and capable of providing high - quality 
clinical data.
According to the inclusion and exclusion criteria, a 
total of 1,884 AP patients were finally included in this 
study for data analysis. The number of samples from each 
hospital is shown in Table 1.
Inclusion criteria: Ⅰ. Age ≥ 18 years old; Ⅱ. First - onset 
and diagnosed with AP; Ⅲ. Complete clinical data; 
Ⅳ. Admitted to the hospital within 24 h after the 
onset of the disease. Exclusion criteria: Ⅰ. History 
of severe liver or kidney function abnormalities; 
Ⅱ. Complicated with infectious or metabolic 
diseases; Ⅲ. Complicated with malignant tumors; 
Ⅳ. Secondary cases of acute pancreatitis such as 
postoperative pancreatitis; Ⅴ. Lack of key laboratory 
test data; Ⅵ. Pregnant state.
Data collection
Demographic characteristics, clinical features, and labo­
ratory examination indicators were extracted from elec­
tronic medical records. The demographic information 
included basic data such as the patients’ age, gender, 
weight, and height. Clinical features consisted of the 
admission time, length of hospital stay, past medical his­
tory (e.g., diabetes, hypertension), and comorbidities.
The laboratory examination indicators were divided 
into two parts. One part included the examination indi­
cators within 48  h after the patients’ admission, which 
were used to construct an early prediction model for 
early intervention. The other part included the examina­
tion indicators within 72 h after admission, which were 
used to build a more accurate prediction model. The 
detailed information of the patients’ data is shown in 
Table 2.
Protocol design
Federated learning technology

mented on the Arya privacy computing platform to 
enable cross-center collaborative modeling while pre­

Two prediction protocols
Protocol 1: It was based on the laboratory examination 
indicators within 48 h after the patients’ admission, 
aiming to achieve early prediction and facilitate early 
intervention by clinicians. Since some indicators 
may not show significant abnormalities in the early 
stage, the prediction accuracy of Protocol 1 might be 
relatively low.
Protocol 2: It was based on the examination indicators 
within 72 h after the patients’ admission, aiming to 
improve the prediction accuracy.
Contribution Evaluation Algorithm: This algorithm 
was used to evaluate the contributions of each 
participating center in the joint modeling process. 
By monitoring the changes in model performance 
after each iteration, the actual contributions of 
each center’s data to the model improvement were 
quantified, thus achieving a more objective and fair 
contribution evaluation.
Data processing
Data Filling: Not all patients have complete data, which 
leads to unfilled items or missing values in the 
dataset. The higher the proportion of missing data, 
the more difficult it is to recover the information of 
the original data, and the more likely it is to affect 
the performance of the model. The calculation of the 
missing rate is mainly divided into two parts.
The first part is the missing rate of features in samples, 
that is, the proportion of missing indicator values in each 
row of the local dataset matrix. This part is calculated 
locally by each participant, and samples with a missing 
rate that does not meet the requirements are excluded. 
The second part is the feature missing rate, referring 
to the global dataset. If the proportion of null values in 
a certain column of the data matrix exceeds 50% of the 
total number of samples, this column will be deleted. 
Generally, features are first filtered according to the 
missing rate, and then samples are filtered according to 
the missing rate. After screening, a total of 51 indicators 
were selected for model training and testing, as shown in 
Table 2.
For the samples with missing values, the method of 
group - mean filling was adopted. The data were grouped 
according to the label categories, and then the within - 
group mean was calculated as the filling value to replace 
the missing values within the group, so as to maintain the 
consistency and integrity of the data and avoid additional 
noise or bias, as shown in Table 3.
Data Standardization: The z - score method was used 
for data standardization, transforming the data 
into a distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard 
deviation of 1. This process required calculating 
the mean and standard deviation of each indicator. 
Subsequently, each indicator value was transformed

Data standardization helps eliminate the dimensional 
differences between different indicators, enabling the 
model to more easily capture the relative change rela­

and generalization ability of the deep - learning model, 
and provide more stable and balanced input data for the 
model. During the model deployment phase, the input 
data still needs to be standardized based on the mean and 
standard deviation calculated during training to ensure 
that the features input into the model are consistent with 
those in the training process.
Model design
In this study, two machine - learning methods were 
employed to construct a prediction model for the sever­
ity of AP patients, namely Logistic Regression (LR) and 
Deep Neural Network (DNN). Two prediction protocols 
were designed, incorporating laboratory examination 
indicators within 48  h and 72  h after admission 
respectively.
LR is a statistical model widely used in binary classifi­
cation problems. It makes predictions by estimating the 
linear relationship between features and outcomes. The 
DNN uses a Multi - Layer Perceptron (MLP) structure, 
which can capture complex non - linear relationships 
in the data, enhancing the flexibility and accuracy of 
prediction.
For the Deep Neural Network (DNN) architecture, 
we specifically adopted a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) 
structure. This choice is primarily driven by the nature 
of our data—tabular clinical indicators (e.g., laboratory 
test results, demographic characteristics) which form the 
core of our input features. MLP is well-suited for cap­
turing non-linear relationships within such tabular data, 
as it does not require prior assumptions about spatial 
or sequential patterns (unlike convolutional neural net­
works optimized for image data or recurrent neural net­
works for time-series data).
Additionally, considering the federated learning frame­
work and multi-center collaboration, MLP’s relatively 
lightweight structure reduces computational and com­
munication overhead during cross-institutional param­
eter aggregation. This efficiency is critical for balancing 
model performance and practical feasibility in a distrib­
uted setting with privacy constraints. Its simplicity also 
mitigates the risk of overfitting to institution-specific 
data distributions, enhancing the generalizability of the 
aggregated global model across participating centers.
Both prediction protocols used the above two machine 
- learning methods for modeling to ensure the consis­
tency and comparability of the models under different 
time windows. Finally, by comparing the performance of

Contribution evaluation module
The contribution evaluation method for federated mod­
eling consists of two modules: the data contribution eval­
uation module and the model contribution evaluation 
module.
Data Contribution Evaluation Module: The data 
contribution evaluation module assesses data from 
two aspects: data volume and data quality. Regarding 
data quality, we mainly refer to three dimensions, 
namely timeliness, completeness, and scarcity [14]. 
These three dimensions are also the three most 
important and concerning aspects of medical data. 
Different weights are assigned to different values of 
each sample in these dimensions.
Timeliness: For data that is over 13 years old, we believe 
it has little significance for model - building, so no 
weight is assigned to such data.
Completeness: This mainly takes into account the 
missing situation of each feature dimension in each 
sample. We calculate the coverage rate of sample 
features, and different weights are assigned to 
samples with different coverage rates.
Scarcity: This mainly considers the scarcity of samples 
participating in the model - building. Globally, 
moderately severe and severe acute pancreatitis 
patients account for 20% of all acute pancreatitis 
patients. Therefore, for the classification task of 
acute pancreatitis severity, samples of severe acute 
pancreatitis are scarcer. The features and weights of 
the data are shown in Table 4.

Results
Baseline information
The data used in the study were from a total of 1,884 
patients. The data originated from 4 hospitals. The 
median age was 50 years old (range: 18–85 years). There 
were 1,025 male patients and 859 female patients. The 
median body mass index was 21.3  kg/m² (range: 14.5–
32.4 kg/m²). Among them, there were 935 patients with 
severe acute pancreatitis and 949 patients with mild 
acute pancreatitis. The data included 51 physical indica­
tors of the patients.
Model evaluation results
For the testing set performance under the 48-hour pro­
tocol: The logistic regression (LR) model achieved sen­
sitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 78.70%, 72.90%, and 
75.90%, respectively, while the deep neural network 
(DNN) model showed better performance with 78.20% 
(sensitivity), 78.40% (specificity), and 78.30% (accuracy).
Under the 72-hour protocol (testing set results): The 
LR model yielded 83.30% (sensitivity), 70.60% (specific­
ity), and 77.10% (accuracy), whereas the DNN model 
outperformed it with 78.10% (sensitivity), 80.90% (speci­
ficity), and 79.40% (accuracy).
Notably, the 72-hour protocol models demonstrated 
the highest overall accuracy, and across both time win­
dows, the DNN model emerged as the optimal choice. 
See Table 5 (explicitly labeled with “Training” and “Test­
ing” columns) and Fig. 2 for detailed comparisons.

Discussion
Severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) is a critical condition of 
pancreatitis, accounting for approximately 20% − 30% of 
cases and accompanied by persistent organ dysfunction 
[15]. Modern medicine views pancreatitis as a dynami­
cally evolving process. Therefore, there is a need for a 
simple and practical prediction model to forecast the 
occurrence of SAP at an early stage, enabling targeted 
and standardized treatment in advance, shortening 
the patient’s disease course, and reducing the mortal­
ity rate. Compared with traditional statistical methods, 
machine learning can self - learn from complex clinical 
data, analyze the hidden patterns behind the complex 
data, identify indicators related to clinical outcomes, and 
establish mathematical models. These models can also be 
repeatedly calibrated during the validation process [16]. 
However, due to the limitations of single - center data, 
clinical prediction models constructed based on them 
often show poor accuracy and reliability during external 
validation, that is, when tested in other medical institu­
tions or different patient populations. The models may 
not adapt well to the patient characteristics and medi­
cal data distributions in new environments, resulting in 
inaccurate prediction results [17] The federated learning 
algorithm constructs a global model by aggregating the 
local model parameters of multiple participating parties. 
While protecting the data privacy of each party, it enables 
data sharing and collaborative model training. To obtain 
a model with better performance in global training, it is 
necessary to conduct performance verification and evalu­
ation on the selection of local models [18].
Currently, in the practice of joint modeling in the medi­
cal field, the existing contribution evaluation methods 
have obvious limitations, mainly manifested in the lack of 
an effective evaluation mechanism and the simple evalua­
tion based solely on the data volume. To address these 
issues, this study proposes an evaluation algorithm that 
comprehensively considers data quality and model con­
tribution. This algorithm not only conducts multi - 
dimensional evaluations of quality indicators other than 
data volume (such as timeliness and completeness) at the 
data level but also dynamically adjusts the contribution 
scores of each participating party based on the model 
performance. Specifically, the algorithm quantifies the 
actual contributions of each center’s data to the model 
improvement by monitoring the changes in model per­
formance after each iteration, thereby achieving a more 
objective and fair contribution evaluation. This approach 
can effectively reflect the real value of each center in the 
model training process and promote fair cooperation and 
resource sharing among multiple centers. The multi - 
center prediction model for the severity of acute pancre­

[19] This superiority is mainly attributed to the powerful

of the DNN. The pathogenesis of acute pancreatitis (AP) 
is complex, involving multiple physiological and patho­
logical processes and numerous influencing factors, and 
there are highly non - linear relationships among these 
factors. Through multiple hidden layers, the DNN can 
automatically learn complex feature representations from 
a large amount of clinical data, uncover the hidden pat­
terns and rules behind the data, and thus more accurately 
capture the information related to the disease severity. In 
contrast, as a linear model, the LR has relatively limited 
ability to learn data features. It mainly relies on manual 
feature design and selection and has difficulty fully min­
ing the complex information in the data. When dealing 
with complex diseases like AP, its prediction ability is 
restricted to a certain extent [20].In terms of the model’s 
generalization ability, the DNN also demonstrated excel­

where there were certain differences in patient character­

among different centers. This posed high requirements 
for the generalization ability of the model. The DNN 
model could well adapt to the heterogeneity of this multi 
- center data and maintain relatively stable prediction 
performance on the data from different centers. This was

large - scale data training process, enabling it to effec­
tively process and predict data with different distribu­
tions. On the contrary, when faced with multi - center 
data, the LR model might experience a decline in perfor­
mance due to the differences in data distribution, indicat­
ing that its generalization ability was relatively weak. Our 
study also found that the model constructed using exami­
nation indicators within 72 h after admission had more 
stable performance than the one constructed within 48 h 
after admission. Similar results were also shown in previ­
ous studies [21]. This is because indicators such as blood 
amylase, blood lipase, and C - reactive protein (CRP) 
start to change after 48 h. Therefore, indicators at 72 h or 
even later may be more meaningful for judging the sever­
ity of the disease [22]. Notably, previous studies have 
shown that there is no significant difference in the out­
comes between interventions at 72 h and those at 48 h 
[23]. Thus, this study not only further validates the 
important value of the 72 - hour time point in the diag­
nosis and treatment process of acute pancreatitis but also 
provides more time flexibility for clinical treatment deci­
sions. The differential performance of deep neural net­
works (DNN) and logistic regression (LR) across both 
48-hour and 72-hour protocols reflects their inherent dif­
ferences in modeling complex clinical data—with direct 
implications for clinical decision-making. LR, a linear 
model, estimates relationships between features and out­
comes through a straightforward linear combination of 
variables. This simplicity limits its ability to capture the 
non-linear, dynamic interactions that characterize acute 
pancreatitis (AP) pathogenesis. For example, AP severity 
depends on intertwined changes in inflammatory mark­
ers (e.g., C-reactive protein [CRP] rising beyond 48  h), 
hematological indices (e.g., hematocrit [HCT] and blood 
urea nitrogen [BUN] fluctuations), and organ function 
indicators—relationships that are not strictly linear. LR’s 
reliance on linear associations explains its lower specific­
ity across both time windows: in the 48-hour protocol, 
LR’s specificity (72.90%) was 5.5% lower than DNN’s 
(78.40%); in the 72-hour protocol, this gap widened to 
10.3% (70.60% vs. 80.90%). Lower specificity increases the 
risk of overclassifying mild AP as severe, potentially lead­
ing to unnecessary aggressive interventions (e.g., pro­
longed ICU stays or unwarranted antibiotics). In 
contrast, DNN’s multi-layer perceptron structure excels 
at decoding non-linear relationships by automatically 
learning hierarchical feature representations. This allows 
it to integrate subtle patterns—such as the delayed corre­
lation between post-admission triglyceride levels and 
pancreatic necrosis, or the interplay between age, BMI, 
and CRP dynamics—that LR misses. Clinically, this 
translates to more balanced performance: DNN main­
tained higher accuracy (78.30% in 48 h, 79.40% in 72 h) 
compared to LR (75.90% in 48  h, 77.10% in 72  h) and 
reduced overdiagnosis risk, aligning with the need to bal­
ance sensitivity (avoiding missed severe cases) and speci­
ficity (avoiding unnecessary treatment). The superior 
performance of the 72-hour protocol (across both mod­
els) underscores the importance of temporal biomarker 
evolution in AP severity prediction—with critical practi­
cal implications for clinicians. Biologically, key AP mark­
ers exhibit delayed changes: CRP, a hallmark of pancreatic 
inflammation, often peaks 72 h after onset, and its sus­
tained elevation (> 150 mg/L) is strongly associated with 
necrosis. Similarly, pancreatic enzyme levels (amylase, 
lipase) and organ function indicators (e.g., creatinine for 
renal status) stabilize by 72 h, providing more reliable sig­
nals than their 48-hour counterparts. This explains why 
the 72-hour DNN—our optimal model—achieved the 
highest accuracy (79.40%), outperforming the 48-hour 
DNN by 1.1%. For clinicians, the 72-hour window offers 
actionable precision. By this time, the model’s improved 
specificity (80.90% for DNN) helps confidently identify 
patients requiring escalated care (e.g., those with severe 
AP needing organ support), while its sensitivity (78.10%) 
minimizes missed severe cases. Importantly, this aligns 
with clinical practice: previous studies [22] note no sig­
nificant difference in outcomes between interventions at 
48 vs. 72 h, meaning the 72-hour window does not delay 
critical care but instead refines decision-making. For 
example, a patient with borderline 48-hour markers (e.g., 
mild CRP elevation) can be reassessed at 72 h using the 
model to confirm severity, avoiding premature escalation 
or discharge. The 48-hour protocol retains value as an 
early screening tool. Its DNN model (78.30% accuracy) 
provides timely initial stratification, helping triage high-
risk patients (e.g., those with rapid BUN rise) for close 
monitoring while the 72-hour data matures. Together, 
the two time windows form a complementary frame­
work: rapid initial assessment followed by a refined, data-
driven confirmation. DNN’s superiority over LR 
highlights the need for non-linear modeling in AP, where 
pathogenesis involves interconnected biological pro­
cesses beyond linear relationships. For clinicians, this 
means a more reliable tool to distinguish mild from 
severe cases, reducing both under- and over-treatment. 
The 72-hour window, meanwhile, empowers clinicians 
with a pragmatic timeline: it balances the need for early 
action with the biological reality that key markers take 
time to manifest. By leveraging 72-hour data, clinicians 
can adjust treatment plans—such as de-escalating care 
for patients reclassified as mild, or intensifying support 
for those confirmed as severe—with greater confidence. 
This aligns with the dynamic nature of AP management, 
where clinical judgment benefits from both timely and 
accurate information. Overall, the model in this study 
offers new ideas and a basis for the clinical diagnosis and 
treatment of acute pancreatitis. It serves as a powerful

patient’s condition, which helps in the early identification

Limitations of the study
This study has several limitations. Firstly, the similarity 
between centers has not been explored currently. This 
implies that further investigations are required to dis­
cover the potential similarities among datasets from dif­
ferent centers. By revealing the common features and 
identifying the domains where the model can effectively 
utilize data from multiple centers, the robustness of the 
proposed method can be enhanced. Secondly, although 
the algorithm adopted in this study comprehensively 
takes into account the data quality and model contribu­
tion of each hospital, it fails to effectively address the 
differences in data distribution among different hos­
pitals. While a more granular subgroup analysis or for­
mal heterogeneity test could provide additional insights, 
such analyses were not included in this work because 
our primary aim was to develop and validate a robust 
multi-center federated model. Instead, heterogeneity was 
considered during evaluation by constructing the test 
set with 20% of the data from each center and applying 
a weighted aggregation strategy during training, which 
helped ensure balanced performance assessment and 
mitigate sample size imbalance. Currently, this study 
is retrospective. It is planned to conduct a prospective, 
multi-center validation in the future, covering a more 
extensive patient cohort. This will strengthen the general­
ization ability of the model using federated learning.
Conclusion
Based on federated learning, this study successfully inte­
grated collective knowledge and data resources from var­
ious medical institutions. Meanwhile, it ensured patient 
privacy and data security, demonstrating a significant 
advancement in using machine learning to predict the 
severity of AP.

Abstract: Background Acute pancreatitis (AP) is a common gastrointestinal disease prone to severe systemic complications, presenting with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis depends on serum markers and imaging. Categorized by the Atlanta classification, about 20% of cases progress to more severe forms. Due to its rapid progression and high misdiagnosis rate, early and accurate assessment is crucial. In this study, we aim to construct a deep neural network to provide a scientific basis for the clinical management of AP. Methods A total of 1,884 patients diagnosed with AP from four hospitals, namely the Fourth Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine(ZJU-H4), the First Affiliated Hospital of Ningbo University(NBU-H1), the Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University(ZCMU-H2), and Lishui People’s Hospital(LISHUI-H), were retrospectively included from 2012 to 2024. The examination indicators of the patients within 48 h and 72 h after admission were collected. Clinical models were developed using Arya, a novel privacy computing platform by Healink to predict the severity of AP in patients. Two learning methods—logistic regression (LR) and deep neural networks (DNN)—were applied within the federated learning framework. Moreover, to address the challenge of fair contribution evaluation in federated learning, a novel assessment method integrating data quality and model performance impact was proposed. Results In the 48-hour scenario, the DNN model showed higher prediction performance than the logistic regression model in terms of sensitivity (78.20% vs. 78.70%), specificity (78.40% vs. 72.90%) and accuracy (78.30% vs. 75.90%); the same trend was observed in the 72-hour scenario: sensitivity (78.10% vs. 83.30%), specificity (80.90% vs. 70.60%) and accuracy (79.40% vs. 77.10%). BMC Gastroenterology (2025) 25:681 Key findings • We constructed deep neural network models using data from 1884 AP patients from four hospitals. In both 48 - hour and 72 - hour scenarios, DNN outperformed logistic regression in predicting AP severity. The DNN - based model using 72 - hour - after - admission indicators was the most accurate. What is known and what is new? • Known: Some serological indicators help evaluate AP severity but have limitations. Existing scoring systems have many items and poor operability. • New: We integrated data from multiple institutions via federated learning on a privacy - computing platform. We also proposed a new contribution evaluation method for fairer federated learning. What is the implication, and what should change now? • Implications: Our study enables more accurate early prediction of AP severity, ensuring patient privacy. The new evaluation method promotes fairer multi - center collaboration. • Actions needed: Clinicians can use our model for better AP manage­ ment. More institutions could adopt federated learning with our evalu­ ation method for future research.
